title: Two witnesses
hook: fifth point: of the two witnesses, others' opinion and your own, trust your own honest one

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five strengths: intention, familiarity, seed, reproach, aspiration. Your line was five strengths. Did you make a wish before sleep for the good of the day? Day one thousand three hundred one.

Four and a half stars. A restaurant, a plumber, a podcast, a person's whole social feed: a lot of daily life now runs on the ratings of strangers. And it spills over. Did that go well? Check the reactions. Am I a good person? Look at how many people seem to think so. The seven points of mind training reach a question every practice has to face sooner or later: how would you know it's working? Point five gives several answers, and one of them puts the ratings in their place. Today, two witnesses.
screen: `FOUR AND A HALF STARS.` → `LIVING BY STRANGERS' RATINGS.` → `HOW WOULD YOU KNOW IT'S WORKING?`

segments.voice: First, one measure. A slogan of point five says, in effect, that all the teachings agree at one point. The commentaries name the point: is self-cherishing getting smaller? Not visions, not hours logged. Is the me-first reflex a little quieter than it was? Second, the two witnesses. One is other people's opinion of you. The other is your own. The slogan says to hold the principal one, and the commentaries say the principal one is your own. Others see only the outside. They can be fooled by a calm face, and they can miss a quiet effort entirely. Only the one acting was there for the motive: the flash of envy let go, the kindness done partly for show. Third, the honest witness. This is not permission to grade yourself kindly. The witness has to be honest, or it's just a fan. The older suttas have a picture for this. In a discourse to his son Rahula, the Buddha compares checking an action to looking in a mirror: before you act, while you act, and after, ask whether it harms yourself or others. A mirror doesn't flatter and doesn't scold. It shows. Fourth, two other signs from point five. One slogan says to keep a joyful mind, steady rather than giddy. Another says that if you can practice even when distracted, you are well trained, the way a good rider stays on when the horse shies. None of these need an audience. Others' praise is pleasant. Others' blame stings. Neither one is the witness that counts here.
screen: `ONE MEASURE: LESS ME FIRST.` · `TWO WITNESSES: THEIRS AND YOURS.` · `THE HONEST WITNESS IS A MIRROR.` · `JOY, AND PRACTICE WHEN DISTRACTED.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN WITNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check yourself honestly. Sit and let the breath settle. Pick one moment from the past day, something you said or did with another person. Hold it up like a mirror. What did it look like from outside? Then, what was underneath it: the real motive, as best you can see it. Don't defend it and don't punish it. Just see it. Then ask the one question point five cares about: was the me-first reflex louder or quieter in that moment? Let the answer be whatever it is. The bell holds the time.
Two witnesses. Others' opinion of you, and your own honest one. Point five says to hold your own. Today's word.
Your line: your own witness. Today, when you catch yourself checking how something landed with others, ask the mirror question instead: what was my motive? Day one thousand three hundred one.

howItsDone: Practitioners of Tibetan mind training assess their practice by point five's measures, chiefly whether self-cherishing is lessening, and rely on their own honest self-examination rather than others' praise or blame.

myth: the principal witness is other people's opinion
the commentaries say it's your own honest view, since only you see your motives.
trusting your own witness means grading yourself kindly
the witness has to be honest, like a mirror that neither flatters nor scolds.
a slogan says practicing even when distracted is a sign of training
like a good rider who stays on when the horse shies.

fork.setup: you did something kind, and everyone praised you. but you know part of you did it for show. which witness does point five tell you to hold?
options: the crowd: they all thought it was kind.
your own honest view of the motive.
fork.reveal: of the two witnesses, hold the principal one: your own, because only you were there for the motive.

trapdoor: what you thought: trust yourself, ignore the haters.
what it means: point five: others see the outside; your own honest view sees the motive, so it's the principal witness.
what a scholar hears: one of several tests in point five, alongside the single measure that all teachings agree on: lessening self-cherishing.

notes: Point five slogans are paraphrased without quotation marks (English renderings are modern). Confirm they fairly render the Tibetan.
'The commentaries say the principal witness is your own' follows the index line; confirm.
The good-rider image for practicing when distracted is offered as illustration; some commentaries use a similar image. Confirm or cut.
